title: Praying With the One You Disciple
subtitle: Four sessions on teaching someone to pray by praying with them, plainly and out loud
summary: Nobody learns to swim from a chalkboard. You learn in the water, with someone beside you who has done it before. Prayer is the same. The disciples did not ask Jesus for a lecture on prayer. They watched him pray and asked him to teach them how. This study is four short sessions for two people, the one discipling and the one learning, and it ends every time the only way prayer is ever really learned, by actually praying together out loud before you leave the table. It moves from the disciples asking to be taught, to the pattern the Lord gave as a frame to fill, to praying out loud without fear because the Father already knows, to carrying the other person to God and letting them hear you do it.
setting: A quiet enough table that you can pray out loud together without performing for a room. A kitchen, a coffee shop corner, a porch. Somewhere the two of you can hear each other and God can hear both of you.
forWho: Anyone discipling a person who does not yet know how to pray or is afraid to pray aloud, and the person learning. New believers, old believers who never learned, anyone who freezes when it is their turn to pray.
rhythm: Four sessions, short, always ending by actually praying together out loud before you leave the table. Once a week over a meal or a coffee works well.
leaderNote: Teach prayer the way you teach a child to swim, in the water, not on a chalkboard. Pray plainly and briefly in front of them so they hear that God is not grading. Most people who are afraid to pray out loud are afraid because the only prayers they ever heard were long and polished and made by professionals. Break that spell by going first and going short. Every session ends with them praying one real sentence out loud. Do not correct it. Do not improve it. The point of the first sentence is that it happened.

sessions.title: Lord, Teach Us to Pray
sessions.bigIdea: The disciples spent years around Jesus and asked him for exactly one skill by name, how to pray. They did not want a definition. They wanted to learn to do what they had watched him do, and they knew the way in was to be shown.
sessions.open: When someone says lets pray, what happens inside you? Relief, dread, a blank mind, a fear you will say it wrong? Say it honestly. This whole study starts there.
sessions.read: Read Luke 11:1 out loud. Now Jesus was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him, Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples. Notice the order. Jesus prays first, where they can see it, and only then does someone ask to be taught. The lesson began before a word of instruction was ever spoken.
observe: What were the disciples doing right before one of them asked the question? What had they just watched?
They did not ask for a book or a rule. What exact words did they use for what they wanted?
talk: The disciples had heard Jesus teach for a long time, but prayer was the thing they asked to be taught by name. Why do you think prayer is the part people most want help with and most rarely ask for help with?
One of them was brave enough to admit out loud that he did not know how. What would it cost you to say the same thing at this table right now, that you do not really know how to pray?

The learner and the one teaching are both at this table on purpose. To the one learning, what do you hope to be able to do by the end of these four weeks? To the one teaching, tell them plainly, you did not always know how either.
sessions.practice: Before you leave the table tonight, the one teaching prays out loud first, short, thirty seconds, in plain words, so the learner hears what unpolished prayer sounds like. Then the learner prays one sentence out loud. Anything true. Even God, I do not know how to do this, is a real prayer and God has heard it gladly.
sessions.send: The disciples did not wait until they were good at it to begin. They asked, and Jesus taught them by letting them start. You started tonight.
sessions.passItOn: The one learning this week: tell one person that you are learning to pray and that it is not too late and not too hard. Someone near you is carrying the same fear and has never said it out loud.

sessions.title: The Pattern He Gave
sessions.bigIdea: When they asked how to pray, Jesus did not hand them a script to recite. He gave them a shape to fill, a few short lines that name who God is, what the day needs, and where we fall short. It is a frame you can hang your own words on.
sessions.open: Say the Lords Prayer together from memory if you both know it, or read it slowly if you do not. Then be honest, when you have prayed it before, did it feel like talking to God or like reciting something?
sessions.read: Read Matthew 6:9-13. Pray then like this. Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. Notice how short it is. There is room in every line for your own life to be poured in.
observe: Jesus says pray then like this, not pray then these exact words. What is the difference between a script and a pattern?
Walk the lines in order. Where does the prayer start, with God or with us? What does it ask for before it asks forgiveness?
talk: The prayer opens with who God is before it asks for anything. Most of our praying starts with what we want. What would change if you spent the first ten seconds just naming who God is before you brought him a single request?

Give us this day our daily bread is permission to bring God the ordinary and the small, todays lunch, todays worry, todays bill. What is one plain daily thing you have never thought was big enough to pray about?

Try it live. Take one line of the pattern, your kingdom come, and fill it with your own life out loud. Where in your world do you want God to be king this week? That is praying the pattern, not reciting it.
sessions.practice: This week, pray the pattern once a day, but stop at each line and put your own words in. Our Father, and say what it means to you that he is a father. Give us bread, and name the day you need. The one learning does this on their own once, then reports back next time what it was like to fill the frame.
sessions.send: Jesus did not give you words to hide behind. He gave you a shape to be honest inside. Fill it with your real life.
sessions.passItOn: Teach the pattern to one other person this week the way it was taught to you, as a frame to fill and not a script to recite. A tool this small travels fast, and teaching it is how you learn it.

sessions.title: Praying Out Loud Without Fear
sessions.bigIdea: The fear of praying aloud is the fear of saying it wrong. Jesus pulls that fear out by the root. The Father is not counting your words or grading your grammar. He knows what you need before you open your mouth, so you are free to be short and plain and honest.
sessions.open: What is the worst that could happen if you prayed out loud and it came out clumsy? Say the fear plainly. Then ask, who exactly are you afraid of disappointing, God or the person listening?
sessions.read: Read Matthew 6:7-8. And when you pray, do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words. Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him. The people who piled up words thought volume was the way in. Jesus says the Father was already listening before the first word.
observe: Why did the pagans use so many words? What did they believe more words would buy them?
What does the Father already know before you ask him anything? What does that do to the pressure to say it just right?
talk: A lot of us learned prayer from people who were good with words, and we decided we could never measure up. How did the polished prayers you grew up hearing make you feel about your own?
If the Father already knows what you need before you ask, then prayer is not informing God or impressing him. What is it for, then? What is actually happening when you pray?

Short and honest beats long and false every time. The one teaching prays one plain sentence out loud right now, on purpose, as short as you can make it. Then talk about it, did anything bad happen? Did God mind?
sessions.practice: All week, pray out loud, even when you are alone, in one or two sentences, in the same voice you use to talk to a friend. No special words, no special tone. The one learning prays out loud in front of the one teaching before you part tonight, one honest sentence, and nobody corrects it.
sessions.send: The Father heard your clumsy sentence exactly as gladly as any sermon. You were never being graded. Pray short and pray out loud.
sessions.passItOn: Find one person who freezes when it is their turn to pray, and tell them what you learned, that the Father knows before we ask, so short and plain is not second best. Free somebody the way you were freed.

sessions.title: Carrying Them to God
sessions.bigIdea: Prayer is not only for yourself. Paul never stopped praying for the people he loved, and he told them so. When you pray for the person you are discipling and let them hear you do it, they learn two things at once, how to pray for others, and that they are carried.
sessions.open: Has anyone ever told you they were praying for you, or better, prayed for you out loud with you there? What did it do to you to hear your own name lifted to God?
sessions.read: Read Colossians 1:9. And so, from the day we heard, we have not ceased to pray for you, asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding. Paul carried these people to God constantly and made sure they knew it. Then read James 5:16. Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working. Praying for each other, out loud, is how a healed people are built.
observe: How often did Paul say he prayed for the Colossians? What did he ask God to give them, more stuff or more understanding?
James ties two things together in one sentence, confessing to one another and praying for one another. Why might those two belong side by side?
talk: Paul told people he was praying for them. He did not keep it a secret. What holds you back from saying those words to someone, and what might it mean to them to hear it?

Notice what Paul actually prayed for, that they would know Gods will and grow in wisdom, not just that their problems would go away. When you pray for someone, do you tend to pray for their comfort or for their growth? What would it look like to pray both?

The whole point of these four weeks was never just your own prayer life. It was to make you someone who prays for others out loud. Who is one person, besides each other, that you will start carrying to God by name?
sessions.practice: The one teaching prays out loud for the one learning right now, by name, at the table, the way Paul prayed, for their growth and not only their comfort. Then the one learning prays out loud for the one teaching. Hearing your own name lifted to God is the lesson. This week, each of you prays out loud for one other person, with that person there if you can.
sessions.send: You did not learn to pray only to talk to God about yourself. You learned so you could carry other people to him and let them hear it. Go carry someone.
sessions.passItOn: This is where it comes full circle. The one who was learning becomes the one who teaches. Find a person who does not know how to pray, sit at a table, and do for them exactly what was done for you, pray in front of them, short and plain, and end by getting one honest sentence out of them.
